label: Build vs. buy
question: Should we build or buy AI search for our SaaS product?
context: We are a 6-person engineering team with an 8-week launch target and a $25,000 initial budget. Search is a supporting feature. Assume a managed vendor costs $1,200/month, while a custom build costs $22,000 upfront and $300/month to operate. These are planning estimates, not vendor quotes.

strategist.rationale: Search supports the product rather than defining it. With six engineers and eight weeks, spending the launch window on infrastructure would delay customer learning.
assumptions: A vendor meets baseline relevance and access-control needs.
Search is not the primary product differentiator.
risks: Usage pricing may rise with adoption.
Switching vendors becomes expensive without an adapter.

engineer.rationale: Use a stable internal search contract and keep ingestion under your control. The managed path costs $14,400 in year one versus $25,600 for the custom estimate, excluding integration and migration costs.
assumptions: Supplied cost estimates use the same currency.
Both options can satisfy existing data-access rules.
risks: Vendor-specific ranking can leak into the application.
Integration effort is not included in the cost estimate.

skeptic.rationale: A fast launch is only useful if results are relevant and data boundaries hold. Run an evaluation on representative queries before signing a long contract.
assumptions: A representative query set can be assembled before launch.
A short vendor trial is available.
risks: A demo can hide weak relevance on real queries.
Contract and data-residency terms may block adoption.

strategist.challenge: A custom build offers control, but consumes most of the launch window.
strategist.concession: The skeptic is right: speed does not excuse untested relevance.
strategist.revised_position: Buy only after a short evaluation with explicit acceptance criteria.

engineer.challenge: The strategist underestimates vendor-specific integration work.
engineer.concession: A managed backend has the lower supplied first-year estimate.
engineer.revised_position: Build the adapter and evaluation harness; rent the search backend.

skeptic.challenge: The cost comparison omits migration work and future usage growth.
skeptic.concession: The engineer’s adapter reduces a meaningful part of the exit risk.
skeptic.revised_position: Support a time-boxed pilot with an export test and a clear exit condition.

memo.title: Buy the capability. Own the experience.
memo.recommendation: Start with managed search behind a provider-neutral interface.
memo.summary: Your constraint is time to useful customer feedback. A managed service gets search in front of users sooner, while a thin integration layer keeps a future migration practical. Reassess after the pilot produces real relevance and usage data.
agreement: Use the launch window to validate customer value.
Keep application code independent of the search provider.
disagreements: How much customization will relevance require?
Will usage growth erase the managed service’s cost advantage?
next_steps: Create a 50-query evaluation set with expected results.
Run a two-week managed-search pilot behind an adapter.
Measure relevance, p95 latency, access isolation, and projected spend.
memo.revisit_when: Revisit if the pilot misses relevance targets, required controls are unavailable, or usage makes the build estimate more attractive.
